cells.tense: Here, right now, you are steering this, and someone else's state is part of what you're reading.
cells.act: hold your shape under the weight
cells.ask: Take a load you're already carrying for someone and keep it at its true size this week — don't shrink it to make them comfortable.
cells.core:
When you choose where a day goes, another person's state is real information, and you can take it in without becoming it. You feel where they end and you begin, and that line holds even up close. Direction stays yours while their mood is nearby.

The push toward something is easier when the thing you carry is the thing you meant to carry. Take one load this week — a plan, a worry, a favour — and keep it at its original size instead of compressing it smaller for other people's comfort. Nothing about them has to change. The shape that stays standing is the shape you chose, and it holds better when you stop adjusting it.
cells.sheetLine: You can hold the weight and keep your own line.
cells.verb: Feeling with another person, without either of you disappearing into the other
cells.place: A place where you decide what to do next and in which direction

cells.tense: Ahead of you, a feeling that hasn't arrived is already being read off someone's face, and you are choosing from inside it.
cells.act: let the thing end that is already over
cells.ask: There's an open loop with someone — close it with a single call or message, then leave it closed.
cells.core:
What's coming next has already been rehearsed on someone else's face. You choose direction from underneath another person's mood — anticipating a sigh, a silence, a shift — and the line between your day and theirs thins each time. Committing to a plan when you can't tell which feeling is whose is like reaching for tools in the dark.

What's over with this person is over. A conversation, a version of the relationship, a way you've been arranging your week around them — it can be closed by one plain act, no announcement. When you close it, the direction you pick next is yours again. That's the whole move: stop holding the loop open.

cells.tense: You've been standing at a door that already shut, and the direction keeps getting set from there.
cells.act: add a little or take a little away, and sense the difference
cells.ask: Put one real question into a conversation — something you actually want the answer to — and then wait, without filling the gap.
cells.core:
You steer from a place that lost some warmth, and the compass still points back to it. Days get met from behind a screen — fine, functional, thin. Connection with people hasn't stopped; it stays on the surface because the deeper channel would take weight you haven't been offering. What gets built from here is built at arm's length, and that distance is what makes the choices feel so effortful.

One dial is all that's turning. In a single conversation, add a real question — not a check-in, something you actually want to know — and then wait, without filling the gap. You'll feel where the adjustment lands, and that feeling is you coming back on.

cells.tense: The steering happens and nobody signs for it — days move, and no feeling of your own gets counted in.
cells.act: trace the pattern across the last few times
cells.ask: Recall the last few times you rearranged a day for someone, note each in three words on paper, and add nothing to it.
cells.core:
You'd say you aren't a person who feels much. But look at how the week is arranged — the calls you make, the harder thing you take so someone else doesn't have to, the small tilts that keep others steady. Anyone watching would call that care. To you it's just what got done.

The direction you set has a shape, and the shape repeats. Look at the last few times and mark what you actually did — a line each, no feelings required. Seeing a pattern doesn't ask you to feel it or claim it. It only puts you where you can see the direction you keep choosing, which is a direction you can then pick on purpose.
